7.t: Working with data: what the genome contains
q: Calculate the number of protein-coding base pairs in the human genome.
1.5% of 3100 million = about 46 million bp.
Calculate the mean length of coding sequence per human gene.
46 million / 20 000 = about 2300 bp.
Fugu has about as many genes as humans in a genome 8 times smaller. Suggest how.
It has far fewer repeated sequences and shorter introns: much less non-coding DNA between and inside genes.
Explain why E. coli has such a high percentage of coding DNA.
Prokaryote genes have no introns and there are few repeats; a small genome is copied quickly, so there is selection against extra DNA.
Explain why "non-coding" is not the same as "useless".
Non-coding DNA includes promoters and enhancers that control genes, genes for tRNA, rRNA and regulatory RNAs, and telomeres and centromeres.
A cell stops making cyclin B. Calculate the percentage left after 1 hour.
Suggest why it is an advantage for cyclins to be broken down quickly.
The cell cycle can only move on when the cyclin is destroyed, so its level must be able to fall fast, at exactly the right moment.
After DNA damage, breakdown of p53 is blocked. Predict and explain the effect on the cell.
p53 builds up quickly and stops the cell cycle, giving time for repair, or triggers cell death if the damage is too great.
Explain how a cell marks a protein and breaks it down.
Chains of ubiquitin are attached to the protein; the proteasome recognises the tag, unfolds the protein and hydrolyses it to short peptides and amino acids.
Suggest why haemoglobin lasts as long as the red blood cell.
Mature red cells have no nucleus or ribosomes, so they cannot replace proteins; haemoglobin is recycled only when the whole cell is removed.
